title: Excretory System
tagline: Nephron structure, urine formation, kidney failure and dialysis, and the skin as an accessory excretory organ.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Excretion is the removal of nitrogenous metabolic wastes — chiefly urea — from the body. The human kidneys filter blood in about a million nephrons each: the Bowman's capsule catches the filtrate, the proximal tubule reabsorbs useful substances, the loop of Henle concentrates the urine, and the collecting duct delivers it to the bladder. Understanding the nephron explains how urine is formed, how the body conserves water, and what happens when the kidneys fail — leading to dialysis, where a machine performs the same selective filtration. This chapter also covers the skin (sweat: water, salts, small urea) and the lungs (carbon dioxide and water vapour) as accessory excretory organs.

facts.label: Nephron
facts.value: Functional unit of the kidney — one million per kidney

facts.label: Urine
facts.value: ~1.5–2 L/day; water, urea, uric acid, excess salts; pH acidic

blocks.text: Each kidney contains roughly a million nephrons. Blood arrives by the renal artery, branches into arterioles, and enters the glomerulus — a knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule. High pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea out of the blood into the capsule: this is ultrafiltration. Blood cells and proteins are too large to pass and remain in circulation. The filtrate then travels the renal tubule, where selective reabsorption returns nearly all the water, all the glucose and amino acids, and much of the salt to the blood through surrounding capillaries. The loop of Henle descends into the medulla, creating a salt gradient that allows concentrated urine to form when water is reabsorbed under ADH control. The distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune salt and water; the final urine — water, urea, uric acid and excess salts — drains from the collecting ducts into the pelvis, down the ureter to the bladder, and is expelled through the urethra. The kidney therefore performs three operations on the filtrate: filtration at the glomerulus, reabsorption along the tubule, and secretion of wastes from peritubular capillaries into the tubule.

items.meaning: Functional unit of the kidney: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule and renal tubule.
Pressure-driven forcing of small molecules from blood plasma into the Bowman's capsule.
Return of water, glucose, amino acids and salts from the filtrate to the blood.
Nitrogenous waste made in the liver by deaminating amino acids.
Antidiuretic hormone; increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts, concentrating urine.

items: Renal artery -> glomerulus: high pressure forces filtrate of water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea.
Blood cells and proteins stay in the blood — they are too large to filter.
Reabsorption: all glucose and amino acids, most water and salts return to peritubular capillaries.
Loop of Henle builds a medullary salt gradient enabling concentrated urine.
ADH makes collecting ducts more permeable to water -> less water in urine -> concentrated urine.
Final urine: water, urea, uric acid, excess mineral salts; slightly acidic; ~1.5–2 L per day.

items.text: Diabetics pass glucose in urine because their blood glucose exceeds the tubules' reabsorption capacity.
items.note: Normal filtrate glucose is fully reabsorbed — glucose in urine indicates excess blood sugar.

items.text: After heavy sweating, a small volume of very concentrated urine is produced under ADH control.
items.note: Water conservation in action — the same ADH mechanism as desert animals.

blocks.text: When kidneys cannot filter blood adequately, urea and other wastes accumulate — uraemia — and the patient needs either a transplant or dialysis. Haemodialysis circulates the patient's blood through a machine: blood flows through semi-permeable cellophane tubing bathed in dialysis fluid. Urea, uric acid and excess salts diffuse down their concentration gradients out of the blood into the fluid, which contains none of them; glucose and essential proteins remain in the blood because they are too large to cross the membrane; the dialysis fluid is iso-osmotic with blood plasma so no harmful water shift occurs. The cleaned blood is returned to a vein, heparin prevents clotting in the circuit, and the patient needs several sessions per week, each of hours. The machine filters but cannot replace the kidney's hormonal functions — red blood cell production and blood pressure regulation — so dialysis patients often remain anaemic and must also take other medications.

items: Kidney failure: urea accumulates (uraemia); blood pressure regulation and erythropoietin production also fail.
Dialysis principle: diffusion down concentration gradients across a semi-permeable membrane.
Blood is separated from dialysis fluid by cellophane tubing.
Dialysis fluid has NO urea but HAS glucose and salts at plasma concentrations — wastes leave, essentials stay.
Iso-osmotic fluid prevents dangerous water movement into or out of blood cells.
Heparin keeps blood from clotting in the machine; blood is returned to a vein of the arm.
Transplant is the only complete cure; a functioning transplant also supplies the missing hormones.

items.text: Dialysis fluid composition is refreshed continuously so the gradient for urea never disappears.
items.note: If urea built up in the fluid, diffusion would stop — the gradient must be maintained.

items.text: Kidney patients receive injections of erythropoietin to correct anaemia.
items.note: Shows the kidney is an endocrine organ as well as a filter.

learn.title: Skin and lungs as excretory organs

blocks.text: Besides the kidneys, several organs remove excretory products. The skin's sweat glands secrete sweat — water, mineral salts and a little urea — which cools the body by evaporation and incidentally excretes small quantities of waste; this is why sweat is salty. The lungs exhale carbon dioxide and water vapour, wastes of respiration; the rate of CO2 excretion rises automatically with metabolic activity. The liver, while not an excretory duct organ, is central to excretion because it deaminates excess amino acids, converting the toxic amino group into relatively non-toxic urea, which is then carried to the kidneys for excretion. The large intestine excretes bilirubin (a breakdown product of haemoglobin, giving faeces their colour) along with salts and water. Together these accessory routes support the kidneys and become especially important when kidney function is impaired.

items: Skin: sweat = water + salts + trace urea; primarily thermoregulation, incidentally excretory.
Lungs: exhale CO2 and water vapour — the main route for carbon and hydrogen waste.
Liver: deaminates amino acids -> ammonia -> urea; the urea is excreted by the kidneys.
Large intestine: excretes bilirubin, salts and water in faeces.
Sweat is dilute and salty but far too little to replace kidney function.
During kidney failure, alternate routes cannot compensate — dialysis or transplant remains essential.

items.text: Strenuous exercise doubles sweating and breathing — thermoregulation and excretion increase together.
items.note: More metabolism means more CO2 and more heat to dump via sweat.

items.text: Jaundice colours skin and eyes yellow because bilirubin accumulates when liver excretion of it fails.
items.note: A visible sign of an excretory breakdown in the liver.

figures.caption: Figure: Structure of a nephron
figures.description: Renal artery -> afferent arteriole -> glomerulus in Bowman's capsule (filtration) -> proximal convoluted tubule (reabsorption) -> loop of Henle (concentration gradient) -> distal convoluted tubule -> collecting duct -> pelvis -> ureter -> bladder.

figures.caption: Figure: Kidney, ureter and bladder
figures.description: Kidney filters blood from the renal artery; ureter carries urine to the bladder for storage; urethra expels it; urea made in the liver arrives via the blood.

keyPoints: Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes, mainly urea made in the liver by deamination.
Nephron = glomerulus + Bowman's capsule + tubule; ~1 million per kidney.
Urine formation: ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, secretion.
Blood cells and proteins are not filtered — too large to pass the glomerulus.
All glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed; glucose in urine signals excess blood sugar.
ADH increases water reabsorption -> concentrated urine.
Dialysis: diffusion across semi-permeable cellophane against a maintained concentration gradient; iso-osmotic fluid; heparin prevents clotting.
Skin excretes sweat (water, salts, trace urea); lungs exhale CO2 and water vapour.
experimentFocus: Composition of urine tests: biuret (protein — negative), Fehling (glucose — negative in health), urea tests — know why each is normally absent from urine despite being in the filtrate.
Dialysis questions hinge on concentration gradients: name what diffuses OUT (urea, salts) and what stays IN (protein, blood cells, glucose).
ADH scenarios: low water intake -> more ADH -> small volume of concentrated urine; high water intake -> the reverse.
examFocus: Urine formation questions expect the three stages with locations — filtration at glomerulus, reabsorption along tubule, secretion at distal tubule.
For kidney failure, describe the machine's principles (gradient, iso-osmotic, semi-permeable) rather than vaguely 'washing the blood'.
Accessory organs: name ONE product each — sweat with salts, lungs with CO2 — and note the liver's role in MAKING urea.
Structure-adaptation links earn marks: thick glomerular capillary walls and high pressure for filtration; long loops for concentration.

vocabulary.meaning: Functional filtering unit of the kidney.
High-pressure filtration of plasma into Bowman's capsule.
Return of useful filtrate components to the blood.
Nitrogenous waste formed in the liver from deaminated amino acids.
Machine-based diffusion filtering of blood when kidneys fail.
Antidiuretic hormone concentrating urine by increasing water reabsorption.

questions.prompt: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, each performing filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing alveolus (lung) or villus (gut) — those are the functional units of other organs.

questions.explanation: The liver deaminates excess amino acids, converting toxic ammonia into urea, which is transported to the kidneys for excretion.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the kidney — it excretes urea but does not make it.

questions.prompt: In dialysis, substances leave the blood mainly by:
questions.explanation: The dialysis fluid contains no urea, so urea diffuses out of the blood across the semi-permeable cellophane tubing.
questions.commonMistake: Saying filtration under pressure — the machine relies on gradients, with the fluid refreshed to maintain them.

questions.prompt: Which substance is present in the glomerular filtrate but is normally completely reabsorbed?
questions.explanation: All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; its presence in urine indicates blood glucose above the reabsorption capacity (as in diabetes).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing urea — urea is deliberately left in the filtrate as waste.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: sweat contains water, mineral salts and a small amount of ________, while the lungs excrete carbon dioxide and ________.
questions.explanation: Sweat is dilute urine-like fluid excreted by sweat glands; lungs exhale the gaseous wastes of respiration.
questions.commonMistake: Saying sweat excretes salts only — the urea content is the excretory link worth naming.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the hormone ________ increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water, producing a smaller volume of ________ urine.
questions.explanation: ADH causes more water to be reabsorbed from the collecting duct, so urine becomes more concentrated and lower in volume.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the effect — ADH increases reabsorption, it does not increase urine volume.

questions.prompt: Describe the three stages of urine formation with the site of each.
questions.answer: (1) Ultrafiltration: high blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water, glucose, amino acids, urea, uric acid and salts into the Bowman's capsule; blood cells and proteins remain in the blood. (2) Selective reabsorption: as the filtrate passes along the renal tubule, all glucose and amino acids, most water and much of the salt are reabsorbed into the surrounding peritubular capillaries; the loop of Henle and collecting duct allow concentrated urine to form. (3) Secretion: additional wastes, hydrogen ions and excess salts move from peritubular capillaries into the tubule. What remains — water, urea, uric acid and excess salts — is urine, which drains via the collecting duct to the pelvis, ureter and bladder.
questions.explanation: Three named stages with locations; filtration at the glomerulus, reabsorption along the tubule, secretion into the distal tubule.
questions.commonMistake: Calling osmosis the first stage — the glomerular step is pressure-driven ultrafiltration, not osmosis.

questions.prompt: Explain why dialysis fluid contains no urea but does contain glucose and salts, and why it must be iso-osmotic with blood plasma.
questions.answer: The dialysis fluid contains no urea so that a concentration gradient exists across the cellophane membrane, causing urea to diffuse out of the blood and be removed — if urea were present in the fluid, diffusion would stop. It contains glucose and salts at concentrations similar to plasma so that essential substances do NOT diffuse out of the blood; glucose is retained and no harmful loss occurs. The fluid is made iso-osmotic with plasma so there is no net water movement by osmosis across the red blood cell membranes — otherwise cells would shrink (in a hypertonic fluid) or burst (in a hypotonic one), which would be fatal.
questions.explanation: Each component's presence or absence maps to a principle: gradient for removal, matching for retention, iso-osmotic for cell safety.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining only the urea gradient — the glucose/salt retention and iso-osmotic reasons each earn their own marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of haemodialysis, including the composition of the fluid used and one limitation of the treatment.
questions.answer: In haemodialysis, blood is withdrawn from an artery of the patient's arm and passed through a machine containing long semi-permeable cellophane tubing bathed in dialysis fluid. Urea, uric acid and excess mineral salts in the blood diffuse down their concentration gradients across the tubing into the dialysis fluid, which is continuously refreshed so the gradient never disappears. The fluid contains no urea but contains glucose and salts at plasma concentrations, so essential substances remain in the blood, and it is iso-osmotic with plasma, preventing harmful water shifts into or out of blood cells. Heparin is added to prevent clotting in the circuit, and the purified blood is returned to a vein. Limitation: the machine cannot replace the kidney's endocrine functions — it does not restore red blood cell production or blood pressure regulation — so patients remain anaemic, need treatment several times a week, and often require lifelong medication and dietary restrictions.
questions.explanation: Process steps, fluid composition principles, heparin, and a genuine limitation — the anaemia/endocrine point is the strongest limitation answer.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting heparin and the refreshed fluid — both are frequently required for full marks.

questions.prompt: A patient produces unusually large volumes of dilute urine. Explain this in terms of hormone action, and describe how the body would respond to heavy water loss.
questions.answer: Large volumes of dilute urine indicate low levels of ADH (antidiuretic hormone). Without ADH, the collecting duct walls remain relatively impermeable to water, so much of the water in the filtrate is not reabsorbed and passes out as dilute urine — the condition called diabetes insipidus when caused by ADH deficiency. During heavy water loss, osmoreceptors in the brain detect the rising solute concentration of the blood and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and a smaller volume of concentrated urine is produced, conserving body water and returning blood osmotic concentration toward normal.
questions.explanation: The answer links hormone level, duct permeability, urine concentration and the feedback response — each link earns marks.
questions.commonMistake: Describing ADH as making urine dilute — its action concentrates urine by removing water from the filtrate.
